claims.text: Structural stability during catalytic operation is primarily governed by entropy of mixing.
Entropy of mixing influences nanoparticle phase stability at elevated temperatures.
Changing nanoparticle composition while holding the number of elements constant provides a controlled variation in entropy of mixing.
Nanoparticle phase stability is determined by compositional entropy.
Higher entropy of mixing produces greater configurational stability.
Greater configurational stability reduces phase separation under thermal stress.
Greater configurational stability reduces degradation under thermal stress.
Higher-entropy nanoparticles will retain greater structural stability at elevated temperatures than lower-entropy nanoparticles.
Higher-entropy nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance at elevated temperatures than lower-entropy nanoparticles.
Lower-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit phase separation at elevated temperatures.
Lower-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit reduced catalytic activity at elevated temperatures.
The proposed entropy–stability relationship is limited to multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles.
The proposed relationship does not apply to single-element or non-equiatomic systems.
The relationship between entropy of mixing and structural stability may depend on composition and synthesis method.
